whatItMeans: Usability gains can coexist with omitted information. Larger controlled studies should measure correctness, completeness, actual time saved and downstream care.
streamTitle: Oncology AI summaries reduced reported workload but remained incomplete
streamSummary: In a small oncology workflow study, clinicians reported lower workload and about three minutes saved per case, but only 63.6% of AI summaries were complete. Benefits remain exploratory.
attribution: van Koevorden et al. — npj Digital Medicine

questionAndWhy: Do AI, peer, and teacher comments influence students' ability to evaluate and use feedback differently?
whatTheyDid: A ten-week quasi-experimental study compared three intact Chinese university classes totaling 126 second-language writers. Researchers used pre/post feedback-literacy questionnaires and follow-up interviews.
whatTheyFound: The AI and peer-feedback classes improved significantly on some questionnaire dimensions; the teacher-feedback class showed no significant dimension-level change. Groups were intact rather than independently randomized, and the study did not establish durable writing-performance improvements.
whatItMeans: Different feedback sources may support different learner skills. The null teacher-group finding is not proof that teachers are ineffective; course and group differences limit causal claims.
streamTitle: AI and peer feedback improved some feedback-literacy measures in a classroom study
streamSummary: Across 126 students in three intact classes, AI and peer feedback coincided with gains on some self-reported feedback-literacy dimensions; the teacher group showed no significant changes. Assignment was not randomized.
attribution: Yan and Meng — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

questionAndWhy: Why do coding agents succeed or fail when given the same scientific task? Model selection may matter less than the information, time, verification tools, and other conditions in which the model operates.
whatTheyDid: Wiedmann and colleagues tested five configuration dimensions on four scientific tasks requiring agents to find and operate published specialist models. They analyzed over 18,000 execution trajectories, varying task information, reasoning instructions, verification, time budgets, and language-model backbones.
whatTheyFound: About 54% of outcome variance arose from repeated runs with the same configuration. The information provided to an agent had the largest configuration effect. More time helped conditionally, and telling an agent to verify did little to change verification behavior; providing a dedicated verification tool changed it substantially. The benchmark covers four tasks, not every agent use case.
whatItMeans: Agent TEVV should compare complete configurations and repeated runs. Supplying the right evidence and an actual verification mechanism may be more effective than upgrading a model or adding instructions that merely request more careful reasoning.
streamTitle: Agent setup mattered more than model size in a scientific workflow benchmark
streamSummary: An arXiv benchmark varied instructions, information, verification, time limits, and model backbone across four scientific coding-agent tasks and released more than 18,000 trajectories. Roughly 54% of measured outcome variance came from repeating the same configuration, and the information supplied to agents mattered more than model size or time budget. Asking agents to verify had little effect, whereas giving them a dedicated verification tool altered their behavior. The evidence is limited to these tasks, but it reinforces that reliable agents are engineered systems, not just language models.

questionAndWhy: Can combining language, images and emotional signals improve classification of misleading crisis posts?
whatTheyDid: Researchers combined XLM-R text representations, ViT image features, emotion and sentiment models, and a stacked classifier; they evaluated four existing datasets including a Ukraine-related set.
whatTheyFound: Reported accuracies were 94.66% on Fakeddit, 98.23% on Ukraine-GitHub, 98.12% on Weibo and 97.98% on MediaEval. These are retrospective dataset scores, not demonstrated detection during live conflicts.
whatItMeans: Multimodal ensembles may be useful for triage, but reliability claims need temporal and cross-event validation, transparent labeling standards and calibrated field tests.
streamTitle: Conflict-misinformation ensemble reported high scores on four benchmarks
streamSummary: An ensemble using text, imagery and affective features reported 94.66%–98.23% accuracy across four misinformation datasets. Results were benchmark-based and do not establish live conflict performance.

questionAndWhy: How is the U.S. Army finding tactical power systems and less costly interceptors?
whatTheyDid: Army PIT announced its October 12–14 AUSA competitions for low-signature distributed power and lower-cost interceptor concepts, including prize and demonstration stages.
whatTheyFound: The notice detailed planned selection and funding, including five $100,000 power awards and interceptor prizes up to $20 million; it did not establish winners or technical performance.
whatItMeans: Judge later transition by independently tested prototypes, integration and field results, not announced prizes.
streamTitle: Army innovation contests target tactical power and cheaper interceptors
streamSummary: The Army detailed pitch competitions, prototype funding and a 2027 interceptor demonstration path. These are acquisition priorities and planned opportunities, not proof that solutions are field-ready.
attribution: U.S. Army Pathway for Innovation and Technology — announcement

questionAndWhy: Can autonomous AI security analysis find vulnerabilities in critical military messaging applications at scale?
whatTheyDid: DARPA selected Xint to research AI-based source-code, runtime, and binary analysis for military messaging applications.
whatTheyFound: The program selection and early demonstration establish research activity, not validated reduction in deployed vulnerability risk.
whatItMeans: Security automation should be measured by confirmed findings, false positives, remediation time, and residual risk rather than scan volume.
streamTitle: DARPA selected Xint to study autonomous AI security analysis for military messaging software
streamSummary: Xint announced DARPA selection to research autonomous AI application security across messaging software used in military communications. The company cited early vulnerability findings as evidence of capability. The program is a research effort, not proof that automated analysis reduces operational cyber risk. Confirmation quality, remediation, and false-positive burden will determine practical value.

questionAndWhy: Can multimodal social-media data predict body satisfaction similarly across cultures?
whatTheyDid: Researchers combined image and text features and compared predictive relationships across Western and East Asian participants.
whatTheyFound: Predictive features differed across cultural groups rather than forming one invariant body-satisfaction signature.
whatItMeans: A model can predict the same label through different cultural signals; transportability requires subgroup-specific validation.
streamTitle: Body-satisfaction prediction relied on different multimodal signals across cultures
streamSummary: A Scientific Reports study modeled body satisfaction using multimodal social-media information and found that predictive features differed across Western and East Asian participants. The result shows why a single global model can hide culturally specific relationships. Predictive features are not automatically causal mechanisms, and transfer across populations requires direct testing.

questionAndWhy: How can a rapidly expanding research field identify experts and related topics across institutions without relying only on citations or coauthor networks? This is also a problem for multidisciplinary research discovery.
whatTheyDid: Foppiano and colleagues used OpenAlex to collect 189,581 battery-related works. They combined coarse research concepts with LLM-extracted keyphrases, weighted descriptors by recency and authorship role, computed author similarities, and serialized the resulting graph as RDF linked to Wikidata.
whatTheyFound: The prototype produced browsable topical researcher profiles and similarity maps; it was designed for exploration rather than validated prediction of future collaboration. About 30% of source records lacked abstracts, and inherited author-disambiguation and affiliation errors limit reliability. The displayed network focused on a selected author subset.
whatItMeans: The portable method is especially useful for PSYWERX research discovery: combine controlled concepts, extracted terms, persistent identifiers, provenance, and time-aware weights. Missing metadata and identity reconciliation should remain visible rather than hidden by a polished interface.
streamTitle: An OpenAlex knowledge graph mapped 189,581 battery papers into searchable research expertise
streamSummary: A new paper demonstrates a cross-institutional research knowledge graph built from 189,581 battery-related publications in OpenAlex. The system combines broad bibliographic concepts with fine-grained keyphrases, weights topics by publication recency and authorship, and exposes researcher similarities through an RDF/Wikidata-linked interface. It offers a reusable architecture for finding expertise and adjacent topics without depending exclusively on coauthorship. However, about 30% of publications lacked abstracts, and inherited author-identity errors can distort similarity. The current demonstration supports discovery, not reliable prediction of future collaborations.

questionAndWhy: Does confidence itself act like an intrinsic reward that biases later attention?
whatTheyDid: Researchers manipulated or measured confidence during learning and tracked subsequent attention.
whatTheyFound: Higher confidence influenced later allocation of attention in ways consistent with intrinsic reward, beyond objective task value in the tested paradigm.
whatItMeans: Confidence can become part of the learning signal; calibration matters because confidence may shape what information receives future attention.
streamTitle: Confidence behaved like an intrinsic reward that biased later attention
streamSummary: A Nature Human Behaviour study found that confidence can influence subsequent attention in a way resembling an internal reward signal. Participants preferentially allocated attention based partly on prior confidence, not only objective value. This is controlled task evidence rather than a general model of curiosity, but it shows how metacognitive states can alter future information sampling.

questionAndWhy: How do teachers use cultural understanding when making decisions in multilingual classrooms, and what gets in the way?
whatTheyDid: Researchers conducted and thematically analyzed interviews with 16 female trainee teachers from two Israeli colleges, including Hebrew- and Arabic-speaking participants.
whatTheyFound: Participants described reflective reframing, linguistic knowledge and adaptation to pupils, but also constraints from workload and institutional demands. This qualitative study did not test effects on student outcomes.
whatItMeans: Cultural competence may depend on the setting and resources, not just individual traits. The small, context-specific interview sample cannot establish wider effectiveness.
streamTitle: Teachers described cultural intelligence as context-dependent practice
streamSummary: Interviews with 16 trainee teachers linked multilingual teaching choices to reflection, cultural knowledge and institutional constraints. The study identifies experiences, not causal effects on learning.
attribution: Eliyahu-Levi and Gvura — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

questionAndWhy: Can AI judges consistently score conversational success, especially across different judges and spoken human-AI interactions?
whatTheyDid: Züfle and colleagues compared pointwise and pairwise LLM judgments against human ratings on CANDOR conversations. They proposed a small anchor set for calibration and released Voice Arena Goal, 200 task-oriented human-AI and human-agent conversations with pairwise annotations.
whatTheyFound: Pointwise scores correlated moderately with human ratings, while pairwise comparisons suffered from long transcripts and position bias. The new dataset showed a gap between current judges and human discrimination. Calibration placed judges on a shared scale and transferred to the human-AI dataset in their tests; it did not make the judges equivalent to human evaluators.
whatItMeans: Evaluation scores should carry a calibration protocol and a human reference. In PSYWERX-style human-AI assessments, compare stable anchor cases and inspect order effects before treating score differences as substantive.
streamTitle: LLM conversation judges needed anchors to make their scores comparable
streamSummary: Pointwise scores correlated moderately with human ratings, while pairwise comparisons suffered from long transcripts and position bias. The new dataset showed a gap between current judges and human discrimination. Calibration placed judges on a shared scale and transferred to the human-AI dataset in their tests; it did not make the judges equivalent to human evaluators. Evaluation scores should carry a calibration protocol and a human reference. In PSYWERX-style human-AI assessments, compare stable anchor cases and inspect order effects before treating score differences as substantive.

questionAndWhy: How is the United Kingdom framing resilience against hybrid threats when disinformation, cyber activity, sabotage, foreign interference, and new technologies increasingly interact?
whatTheyDid: In a September 10 OSCE statement published September 11, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office outlined a resilience approach combining responsible technology, AI-enabled early warning and data analysis, stronger situational awareness, new legal authorities, sanctions, and international coordination against hybrid threats.
whatTheyFound: The statement argues that the same technologies that improve early warning can also amplify disinformation and hostile activity, and it points to recent UK legal and sanctions measures as part of the response. It is an official policy position, not an evaluation showing that the package has reduced attacks, changed adversary behavior, or improved public resilience.
whatItMeans: The useful development is the system framing: technology, law, intelligence, diplomacy, and public trust are being treated as interacting parts of hybrid-threat resilience. That creates a clearer assessment agenda around detection quality, decision speed, coordination, legitimacy, disruption, and adversary adaptation.
streamTitle: The UK is treating hybrid-threat resilience as a connected early-warning and disruption system
streamSummary: A new UK statement to the OSCE frames hybrid-threat resilience as a connected system spanning AI-enabled early warning, data analysis, cyber defense, foreign-interference law, sanctions and international coordination. The government argues that technology can strengthen situational awareness while also amplifying disinformation, sabotage and other hostile activity. It cites new legal and sanctions tools as part of the response. This is policy architecture, not outcome evidence: the statement does not show that the measures have yet reduced attacks, improved public resilience or changed adversary behavior.

questionAndWhy: How strongly is damage to essential infrastructure associated with disaster mortality across different hazards and income settings, and which infrastructure sectors appear most consequential?
whatTheyDid: Bhattacharyya, Aydin, and Comes scraped 79 Post Disaster Needs Assessment reports covering 79 disasters this century and used a generalized propensity-score method to estimate a hazard-agnostic dose-response relationship between infrastructure damage and mortality while adjusting for measured confounders.
whatTheyFound: The estimated relationship was nonlinear: greater infrastructure damage was associated with sharply increasing mortality, with stronger effects in low- and lower-middle-income countries. Damage to energy, water/sanitation/hygiene, and health infrastructure showed larger mortality associations than damage to transport, communications, or education. The design is observational and its causal interpretation depends on measured-confounder assumptions and the comparability of post-disaster assessments.
whatItMeans: Infrastructure is not just background context for disaster response; loss of specific systems can amplify human consequences. The sector differences can help prioritize resilience investments, but the estimates should be treated as quasi-causal evidence rather than a universal engineering rule for every hazard or country.
streamTitle: Across 79 disasters, infrastructure damage was linked to sharply higher mortality—especially in lower-income countries
streamSummary: A new Scientific Reports study assembled infrastructure-damage data from 79 post-disaster assessments and used generalized propensity scores to estimate the relationship with mortality. Greater damage was associated with a sharply rising mortality burden, especially in low- and lower-middle-income countries. Damage to energy, water and sanitation, and health systems showed stronger mortality associations than transport, communications, or education. The analysis adjusts for measured confounders but remains observational, so its causal interpretation depends on model assumptions and the consistency of the underlying disaster reports.

questionAndWhy: Does incorrect AI advice change whether people admit uncertainty?
whatTheyDid: A preprint tested human responses to AI advice that was sometimes wrong, measuring answer choices and willingness to say they did not know.
whatTheyFound: Exposure to confident but incorrect AI advice reduced use of 'I don't know' in the tested tasks and shifted responses toward the model.
whatItMeans: AI assistance can change confidence expression as well as accuracy; calibration and abstention should be measured separately.
streamTitle: Wrong AI advice reduced people's willingness to say 'I don't know'
streamSummary: A controlled preprint found that confident but incorrect AI advice could reduce people's use of an 'I don't know' option and pull responses toward the model. The result matters because an assistant can alter confidence behavior even when it does not improve knowledge. The evidence comes from bounded tasks rather than consequential field decisions, so transfer to professional settings needs testing.

questionAndWhy: Can changing what older adults emphasize during training improve selective attention?
whatTheyDid: Researchers manipulated instructional emphasis during an attention-training task with older adults.
whatTheyFound: Training effects depended on what participants were asked to prioritize, with selective benefits rather than broad cognitive improvement.
whatItMeans: Instructional framing can change what is learned; transfer should be measured separately from trained-task gains.
streamTitle: Changing training emphasis altered selective-attention gains in older adults
streamSummary: An experiment with older adults found that what participants were instructed to emphasize during attention training changed the pattern of improvement. Benefits were selective rather than evidence of a general cognitive boost. The result is relevant to training design because task instructions can become part of the intervention; transfer beyond the practiced task still needs separate evidence.

questionAndWhy: Can underwater acoustic systems recognize novel classes instead of forcing every signal into a known category?
whatTheyDid: Researchers developed an open-world underwater acoustic detection method and tested known/unknown recognition.
whatTheyFound: The system improved unknown-event detection in benchmark data while retaining classification performance for known classes.
whatItMeans: Open-world recognition is more realistic than closed-set accuracy, but field noise and adversarial conditions still require validation.
streamTitle: Open-world underwater acoustic detection improved recognition of previously unseen signal classes
streamSummary: A Scientific Reports study developed an underwater acoustic detector designed to recognize when a signal does not belong to a known class. The method improved open-world recognition in the tested datasets. This is more realistic than forcing every observation into a closed label set, but ocean noise, sensor differences, and operational adversaries may produce additional failure modes.

questionAndWhy: Causal-discovery methods are increasingly being packaged as general-purpose or pretrained models, but benchmark performance can depend heavily on the kinds of causal systems used for testing. The authors asked whether method rankings remain stable across different causal mechanisms and evaluation settings.
whatTheyDid: Li and colleagues introduced CausalArena, a benchmark that evaluates classical, neural and pretrained causal-discovery methods under one protocol across synthetic structural causal models, semantically grounded operational models, formula-grounded scientific mechanisms and public real-world datasets.
whatTheyFound: Method rankings shifted substantially across causal-model families and evaluation protocols. Strong performance in one benchmark regime did not reliably transfer to another, and the authors highlight overlap between foundation-model pretraining environments and evaluation systems as a potential source of inflated performance.
whatItMeans: A single leaderboard score is weak evidence that a causal-discovery system will generalize to a new domain. For PSYWERX, the relevant lesson is to validate causal-discovery tools across mechanism types that resemble the intended behavioral or social application and to treat possible training-test overlap as a contamination risk. CausalArena is a preprint, so the benchmark itself still needs external scrutiny.
streamTitle: Causal-discovery rankings changed sharply when the benchmark’s underlying mechanisms changed
streamSummary: A new preprint introduces CausalArena, a benchmark for comparing classical, neural and pretrained causal-discovery methods across several kinds of structural causal systems and public datasets. The authors find that method rankings change substantially across model families and evaluation protocols: a method that looks strong in one benchmark may not transfer to another. They also flag possible overlap between foundation-model pretraining environments and test systems as a contamination risk. The practical lesson is that causal discovery needs mechanism-diverse evaluation, not one leaderboard. CausalArena itself is new and has not yet undergone peer review.

questionAndWhy: Can optimization make chatbot responses more emotionally supportive, and does that imply better user outcomes?
whatTheyDid: Researchers developed EIPO to optimize emotionally supportive chatbot outputs and evaluated response quality.
whatTheyFound: The method improved rated supportive-output characteristics, but the study did not show corresponding changes in user behavior or wellbeing.
whatItMeans: Output quality and behavioral effectiveness are separate evidence stages; a better-looking response is not automatically a better intervention.
streamTitle: EIPO improved emotionally supportive chatbot outputs without demonstrating user behavior change
streamSummary: A Scientific Reports study optimized chatbot responses for emotional support and reported better rated output characteristics. The evaluation focused on the generated responses rather than downstream changes in user wellbeing or behavior. The distinction matters for conversational AI: stylistic or judge-rated improvement is an intermediate outcome, not proof of intervention effectiveness.

questionAndWhy: When an image-classification model is compressed for deployment, do its explanations still point to the same evidence? And can a badly selected explanation layer create a false appearance of model failure?
whatTheyDid: Khandaker compared FP32 and simulated INT8 versions of three image-model architectures on a ten-class, 10,407-image crop-disease dataset. Four explanation methods were evaluated, including 3,240 paired maps per operating point, alongside calibration choices and random-overlap baselines.
whatTheyFound: A naive choice of the last neural-network layer generated constant saliency maps and apparent attribution collapse in as many as 61.7% of images; selecting an appropriate spatial layer eliminated that artifact. Real explanation drift remained model- and method-dependent. INT8 prediction agreement changed sharply with calibration, from about 0.64 under MinMax to over 0.91 under percentile calibration for two models.
whatItMeans: Explainability is sensitive to the entire model and tooling pipeline. Version changes, quantization, calibration, and explainer settings should be recorded before interpreting changed saliency as a substantive shift in what the model learned.
streamTitle: An explainability audit found that a bad layer choice—not quantization—caused many apparent failures
streamSummary: A study of compressed image classifiers compared explanation maps from full-precision and INT8 models across three architectures and four explanation methods. A naive final-layer choice produced constant saliency maps and apparent collapse in up to 61.7% of images; choosing an appropriate spatial layer removed that artifact. Genuine drift still varied by architecture and method, and the choice of quantization calibration strongly affected prediction agreement. The work used agricultural imagery and simulated quantization, so it is not a clinical validation. It demonstrates why explainability claims depend on implementation details as well as the trained model.

questionAndWhy: Can a social platform encourage more open-minded political discussion by changing which behavior earns recognition, rather than trying to change users’ ideology directly?
whatTheyDid: Van Loon and colleagues randomly assigned 1,043 U.S. adults to ten minutes on one of two mobile-app social platforms, with AI-generated discussion partners. One rewarded popularity with a badge; the other rewarded respectful engagement with opposing views.
whatTheyFound: The open-minded-badge condition elicited more intellectually humble language and more positive reported emotion. It did not significantly change self-reported intellectual humility, affective polarization, or issue positions. The encounter lasted ten minutes and used simulated peers.
whatItMeans: Platform incentives can change expressed conversational conduct without changing attitudes. This older but underreported field-relevant experiment is valuable for separating discourse quality, expressed humility, and durable depolarization.
streamTitle: Changing social-platform rewards improved discussion language, not political attitudes
streamSummary: In a randomized app experiment with 1,043 U.S. participants, researchers compared a social platform that rewarded popular posts with one that highlighted respectful engagement across political differences. After a ten-minute conversation with AI-powered participants about immigration or gun control, the open-minded-reward group used more intellectually humble language and reported more positive emotions. However, self-reported humility, affective polarization, and issue attitudes did not significantly change. Although published in July, the study is worth surfacing for its direct test of platform incentives and its clear behavioral-versus-attitudinal distinction.
attribution: van Loon et al. — Scientific Reports

questionAndWhy: If an LLM labels the same texts consistently every time, does that mean it is actually measuring the intended social or political construct? Reproducibility is often used as evidence that automated coding is trustworthy, but reliability and construct validity are different problems.
whatTheyDid: Batzdorfer and colleagues linked free-text submissions from the European Commission’s AI Act consultation to structured survey responses from the same stakeholders. They used LLMs to infer a nominal construct from the text and compared annotation reproducibility with convergence to the stakeholders’ direct survey responses, including differences across stakeholder groups and countries.
whatTheyFound: LLM annotations were extremely reproducible, with intraclass correlations above 0.99, yet they converged only weakly with the survey measure they were intended to approximate. The gap varied systematically: business associations expressed substantially more AI-risk concern in their text than in their survey answers, while several other groups showed smaller or opposite differences. The study is a preprint and does not establish which channel is the uniquely “true” measure.
whatItMeans: A measurement system can be perfectly consistent and consistently measure the wrong thing—or a different context-specific expression of the thing. LLM coding pipelines should validate construct correspondence against external measures and test whether communication setting or stakeholder type changes what the text actually represents.
streamTitle: LLM annotations were almost perfectly reproducible while only weakly matching the construct they were supposed to measure
streamSummary: A new preprint compared LLM coding of European Commission AI Act consultation text with structured survey answers from the same stakeholders. The automated annotations were extraordinarily reproducible, with intraclass correlations above 0.99, but they showed limited convergence with the nominal survey construct. The gap also differed systematically by stakeholder type and country context. The result is a strong warning for automated content analysis: consistency does not establish construct validity. The study is a preprint, and survey answers are not automatically the one true measure, but the mismatch shows why external validation is necessary.

questionAndWhy: Can prior beliefs bias truth processing before deliberate judgment?
whatTheyDid: Four experiments crossed claim accuracy with consistency with participants’ prior beliefs.
whatTheyFound: Belief-consistent falsehoods were accepted more readily, including during automatic validation tasks.
whatItMeans: Misinformation may gain an advantage during comprehension, before explicit reasoning.
streamTitle: Prior beliefs can bias truth processing before deliberate reasoning begins
streamSummary: Across four experiments, people were more likely to accept false claims that matched prior beliefs and reject true claims that conflicted with them. The bias also appeared in a task designed to capture more automatic validation during comprehension. That suggests belief-consistent misinformation may gain an advantage before deliberate defense begins. The studies used controlled claims, not real-world sharing or durable belief change.

questionAndWhy: Can people evaluate how accurate their own decisions are even when they perform the underlying perceptual task well? The study examines metacognition separately from first-order accuracy.
whatTheyDid: Barnby and colleagues compared perceptual choices and confidence ratings across three cohorts of people with corpus callosum dysgenesis, using laboratory, online, and virtual-reality versions of a moving-dot task.
whatTheyFound: Participants with corpus callosum dysgenesis generally achieved normal perceptual accuracy but adjusted confidence less appropriately when task difficulty changed. Computational analyses indicated lower metacognitive sensitivity and efficiency. These comparisons do not prove one isolated neural cause.
whatItMeans: Performance and insight into performance are distinct capacities. Research and training evaluations should measure confidence calibration alongside task accuracy rather than treating correct answers as evidence of self-monitoring.
streamTitle: People with corpus callosum differences judged their own accuracy less reliably despite normal task performance
streamSummary: Across three cohorts and different testing formats, researchers examined people born with corpus callosum dysgenesis, a condition affecting the brain’s main interhemispheric connection. Participants often performed normally on moving-dot perception tasks yet adjusted their confidence less well as difficulty changed. Computational analyses indicated weaker metacognitive sensitivity and efficiency, not simply poorer perception. The result distinguishes task competence from awareness of competence, though observational lesion-group comparisons cannot isolate one neural mechanism or establish how findings generalize to everyday decisions.

questionAndWhy: Can wearable tactile interfaces convey social emotion across virtual reality, mixed reality, and cross-reality encounters?
whatTheyDid: Researchers built a bidirectional social-touch interface with wearable haptic actuators and studied 40 participants organized into 20 dyads in structured emotion-expression and free-interaction tasks across VR and MR conditions.
whatTheyFound: The laboratory comparisons found differences in perceived emotion, embodiment and usability across physical, VR, and MR interactions. Physical touch generally supported stronger affective alignment, while virtual formats involved different trade-offs; the study did not test training outcomes.
whatItMeans: Bidirectional haptics offers a tangible XR affordance for social interaction beyond visual immersion. Transfer to military training, negotiation or influence remains a design hypothesis, not an evaluated effect.
streamTitle: Wearable XR touch conveyed social emotion with VR–MR trade-offs
streamSummary: A 40-person haptic-interaction study compared social-touch communication across physical and immersive settings. Embodiment and emotion judgments varied; training and behavioral transfer were not demonstrated.
attribution: Banerjee et al. — Frontiers in Virtual Reality

questionAndWhy: What consumer-protection problems emerge when AI agents can search, choose, and pay for products on a user’s behalf? Banks are trying to define safeguards before “agentic commerce” becomes routine.
whatTheyDid: A group including NatWest, Bank of America, ING, ASB Bank, Capital One, and Commonwealth Bank of Australia published recommendations on AI shopping agents. They examined payment, scam, fraud, privacy, data-handling, transparency, and platform-interoperability risks.
whatTheyFound: The banks warn that agents could make incorrect purchases, overspend, expose credentials or card data, steer users toward payment methods with weaker protections, or create new scam opportunities. They propose disclosure when AI participates in a transaction, clearer decision transparency, stronger data safeguards, user and merchant choice, and interoperable standards. This is stakeholder risk analysis and proposed governance, not evidence that these harms are already occurring at a measured population rate.
whatItMeans: Agentic commerce changes the unit of consumer protection from a human clicking “buy” to a delegated system acting through several services. Evaluation therefore needs authorization boundaries, identity and disclosure, payment protections, auditability, and clear liability when the agent’s action differs from the user’s intent.
streamTitle: Banks are proposing disclosure and payment safeguards for AI agents that shop on users’ behalf
streamSummary: A group of major banks is warning that AI shopping agents could create new scam, fraud, privacy, payment, and mistaken-purchase risks as agents begin choosing and buying products for users. Their proposed principles include disclosing when AI participates in a transaction, making agent decisions more transparent, protecting customer data, preserving user and merchant choice, and supporting interoperability. This is industry risk analysis rather than measured evidence that the harms are already widespread, but it highlights a concrete governance problem: who is authorized, protected, and liable when an AI agent spends a person’s money.
attribution: NatWest, Bank of America, ING et al. — via Reuters

questionAndWhy: What should a national strategy for military and security AI actually cover?
whatTheyDid: UNIDIR released revised 81-page guidelines on October 19, developed from an earlier draft, government and civil-society feedback, literature review and its AI-security engagements.
whatTheyFound: The guidance separates institutional strategy-development procedures from technical, legal and political considerations across adoption, implementation and review. It is guidance, not a tested policy intervention.
whatItMeans: The structured lifecycle could help compare national AI governance plans; whether it improves responsible deployment remains to be evaluated.
streamTitle: UNIDIR released new national security-and-defence AI strategy guidance
streamSummary: UNIDIR's 81-page October 19 guidelines distinguish strategy-development procedures from technical, legal and political requirements. The document offers governance guidance rather than evidence of policy effectiveness.
attribution: Afina, Mannsperger and Madziwa — UNIDIR guidelines

questionAndWhy: Can pupil dilation track emotional arousal when luminance and attention are changing at the same time?
whatTheyDid: Researchers manipulated visual luminance and attention while participants heard affective sounds and measured pupil response.
whatTheyFound: Pupil dynamics tracked reported arousal across much of the trial, although at least one within-sound analysis was null.
whatItMeans: Pupil size is a mixed physiological signal; arousal interpretation requires controls for light, attention, and timing.
streamTitle: Pupil dilation tracked arousal under controlled luminance, with an important null in one analysis
streamSummary: A pupillometry experiment separated luminance, attention, and affective sound effects. Pupil responses tracked reported arousal across much of the task, but one more specific within-sound analysis was null. The result supports pupil dynamics as one arousal indicator while reinforcing that the measure is influenced by several simultaneous processes.

questionAndWhy: How can a learner pursue rewards without taking dangerous actions while learning? The standard exploration-versus-exploitation framing often neglects the damage an error can cause.
whatTheyDid: Mahajan and Seymour reviewed reinforcement-learning algorithms alongside behavioral and systems-neuroscience research. They organized safety approaches into two families: change the optimization objective to incorporate harm, or constrain exploration so dangerous states and actions are less likely to be visited.
whatTheyFound: The review identifies a recurring safety-versus-learning-efficiency tradeoff. Risk-sensitive objectives can make constraints explicit but require assumptions about costs or uncertainty. Safer-exploration heuristics can limit exposure but may also introduce biases. This is a conceptual synthesis, not a new head-to-head experimental benchmark.
whatItMeans: The distinction between what is optimized and which actions are allowed during learning is useful for human behavior models and autonomous-system design. Harm avoidance should be represented explicitly rather than treated as ordinary reward maximization.
streamTitle: Safe reinforcement learning has two different levers: change the goal or restrict dangerous exploration
streamSummary: A new review links animal learning and neuroscience to the engineering of safe reinforcement learning. It distinguishes changing the objective so harmful outcomes count more heavily from changing exploration so a learner avoids risky actions before it has reliable knowledge. Each approach entails assumptions and a possible tradeoff between safety and efficient learning. The paper synthesizes existing evidence rather than testing a new algorithm. Its practical value is a clearer design vocabulary: an agent can fail because it pursues the wrong objective, because it explores unsafely, or because a protective heuristic becomes overly restrictive.

questionAndWhy: Can many parallel AI research agents cover a large scientific evidence base more effectively than one agent?
whatTheyDid: OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research described a distributed workflow that sent thousands of research agents across an existing mouse-brain perturbation atlas, linking data patterns to scientific literature and having specialists assess selected interpretations.
whatTheyFound: The developers reported broader citation coverage than a single-agent baseline and that masked experts preferred distributed interpretations in 75% of rated comparisons. Proposed biological explanations were hypotheses, not experimentally established mechanisms.
whatItMeans: The concrete transferable idea is parallel, provenance-tracked evidence exploration for large PSYWERX corpora. Faster literature coverage or expert preference would not alone validate an inferred behavioral mechanism or causal claim.
streamTitle: Parallel AI agents expanded literature coverage without validating their hypotheses
streamSummary: A first-party research demonstration used thousands of agents to analyze mouse-brain data and related literature. Expert raters preferred many outputs, but proposed mechanisms await independent experimental validation.
attribution: OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research — primary technical report

questionAndWhy: When social consequences are ambiguous, do people copy self-serving choices made by others?
whatTheyDid: Researchers experimentally manipulated observed social choices and ambiguity around consequences.
whatTheyFound: Self-serving behavior spread under some ambiguous conditions, but effects depended on information and context.
whatItMeans: Behavioral contagion claims should specify the information people observed and the ambiguity surrounding consequences.
streamTitle: Self-serving choices spread more readily when social consequences were ambiguous
streamSummary: A Nature Human Behaviour experiment tested whether people copy self-serving social choices when consequences are not fully clear. Observed behavior influenced later choices under some ambiguous conditions, but the effect depended on what participants could infer from the situation. The finding supports social transmission as one mechanism without implying that selfish behavior automatically spreads in every group.

questionAndWhy: Why do adolescent girls show higher rates of depression and suicidal ideation than boys, and which social or psychological pathways might account for part of that gap? The researchers wanted candidate pathways that could eventually be more actionable than sex itself.
whatTheyDid: Narita and colleagues analyzed 3,171 adolescents in the Tokyo Teen Cohort at ages 12, 14, and 16. Young people helped identify loneliness and desire for thinness as candidate pathways, and the team used a mediational g-formula to estimate how much of the later sex difference was statistically carried through those factors measured at age 14.
whatTheyFound: At age 16, depressive symptoms were reported by 15.9% of girls versus 8.2% of boys, and suicidal ideation by 29.8% versus 18.1%. The model estimated that loneliness and desire for thinness together accounted for 34.7% of the total sex difference in depressive symptoms and 46.3% of the difference in suicidal ideation. These are longitudinal mediation estimates, not randomized tests of changing loneliness or thinness pressure, so they depend on causal assumptions about confounding and measurement.
whatItMeans: The useful contribution is not that two variables “cause” the sex gap, but that a broad demographic disparity can be decomposed into candidate intermediate processes that can be measured and tested more directly. It also shows why mediation estimates should be kept separate from evidence that an intervention on the mediator will improve the final outcome.
streamTitle: Loneliness and pressure for thinness may explain a large share of girls’ higher adolescent internalizing problems
streamSummary: A Nature Human Behaviour study followed 3,171 adolescents in Tokyo from ages 12 to 16 and examined why girls had higher rates of depression and suicidal ideation. A longitudinal mediation model estimated that loneliness and desire for thinness at age 14 statistically accounted for about 35% of the later sex difference in depressive symptoms and 46% of the gap in suicidal ideation. The study identifies plausible intervention targets, but it did not randomize loneliness or body-image pressure; mediation estimates rely on assumptions and should not be read as proof that changing those factors will eliminate the disparity.
attribution: Narita et al. — Nature Human Behaviour

questionAndWhy: Can an AI system code complex human conversations using several established analytic frameworks instead of producing one unsupported summary? Human annotation is expensive, and different codebooks capture different dimensions of interaction.
whatTheyDid: Yang and colleagues built MOSAIC, an agent workflow with codebook selection, retrieval, dynamic examples, annotation, and consistency checking. It was developed with 54 annotated clinical transcripts and evaluated against expert-coded labels on 120 rheumatology and obstetrics/gynecology transcripts.
whatTheyFound: The published evaluation reported an overall weighted F1 of 95.6%, with performance differing across specialty and code category. These are matches against trained coders in two clinical domains, not evidence that the system correctly infers hidden psychological states or generalizes to political and operational dialogue.
whatItMeans: This architecture is directly relevant to PSYWERX corpus coding: preserve each framework’s definitions, retrieve relevant exemplars, maintain auditability, and test disagreement by category. Do not assume high aggregate F1 guarantees performance on rare or interpretive labels.
streamTitle: MOSAIC used multiple codebooks and AI agents to annotate clinical conversations with 95.6% weighted F1
streamSummary: A peer-reviewed study introduced MOSAIC, an agent-based system that chooses communication codebooks, retrieves examples, applies structured annotations, and checks consistency. After development on 54 annotated transcripts, it was evaluated against trained human coders on 120 rheumatology and OB/GYN conversations. The reported overall weighted F1 was 95.6%, although results differed by category and clinical setting. This is a promising design for large-scale qualitative coding, including multi-framework research databases. Its validation does not establish generalization to other kinds of conversations or the accuracy of inferred motives and mechanisms.
attribution: Yang et al. — npj Digital Medicine

questionAndWhy: Can autonomous surface vessels coordinate search, classification, tracking, and replanning as a team?
whatTheyDid: Shield AI and Kraken demonstrated two Hivemind-enabled K3 SCOUT uncrewed surface vessels coordinating an ISR mission using radar, cameras, and AIS.
whatTheyFound: The vessels searched, classified a contact, tracked and escorted it, then replanned and resumed the mission in a demonstration.
whatItMeans: The event demonstrates integration and autonomy behaviors, not contested-environment reliability or mission effectiveness.
streamTitle: Shield AI and Kraken demonstrated two autonomous surface vessels coordinating an ISR mission
streamSummary: Shield AI and Kraken demonstrated two Hivemind-enabled K3 SCOUT vessels searching an area, detecting and classifying a contact, collaboratively tracking and escorting it, and then replanning. The demonstration is meaningful evidence of integrated maritime autonomy, but it does not establish reliability under jamming, adversarial deception, poor weather, or combat conditions.

questionAndWhy: Does time pressure make military decision-makers more likely to over-rely on AI, and how does AI assistance change their sense of moral responsibility? These questions matter as decision-support systems enter high-stakes environments where errors can carry ethical consequences.
whatTheyDid: Salatino and colleagues had military cadets and officers role-play drone operators deciding whether to strike a position, with or without AI support and under high or low time pressure. The AI sometimes gave obviously wrong recommendations so the researchers could observe whether participants followed them.
whatTheyFound: AI assistance increased the likelihood of following wrong and morally questionable recommendations. Contrary to expectations, time pressure alone did not significantly increase AI reliance or change moral decisions. Participants reported less responsibility when using AI, especially under high time pressure, but appeared to recalibrate responsibility when the AI made an obvious error.
whatItMeans: AI over-reliance cannot be reduced to a simple 'time pressure causes automation bias' story. The study suggests that advice quality, perceived responsibility, and human oversight need to be examined separately, and it preserves an important null: more time pressure did not worsen reliance in this particular task.
streamTitle: AI advice increased acceptance of bad recommendations, but time pressure did not make it worse
streamSummary: Military cadets and officers in a simulated drone-strike task were more likely to follow wrong or morally questionable recommendations when AI assistance was present. Unexpectedly, high time pressure did not further increase AI reliance or significantly change the moral decisions by itself. Participants also reported less responsibility when using AI, especially under pressure, while seeming to reclaim responsibility when the system was clearly wrong. The study is a controlled simulation rather than an operational test, so it should not be read as a measured battlefield effect.

questionAndWhy: What happens to the variation and personal signals in human language when people increasingly use LLMs to polish their writing? This matters because language is often used to infer identity, personality, attitudes and social context.
whatTheyDid: Sourati and colleagues combined three studies across seven datasets and more than 880,000 texts. They examined real-world linguistic change alongside controlled LLM rewrites of human-authored text, testing whether meaning was preserved while style and author-linked signals changed.
whatTheyFound: LLM-assisted rewriting largely preserved core meaning but reduced variation in writing complexity by about 21–50% across datasets and models. The rewritten text also weakened some signals used to infer author characteristics and tended to amplify more dominant linguistic patterns while suppressing less common ones. The observational portions cannot prove that every real-world shift was caused by LLM use.
whatItMeans: AI-assisted writing can create measurement drift in any system that treats language as a transparent readout of the person behind it. For PSYWERX, that matters for audience analysis, digital-trace research and any future model that estimates psychological or social attributes from text: the observed language may increasingly reflect both the human and the writing assistant.
streamTitle: AI writing assistants preserve meaning while making human language more alike
streamSummary: A Nature Human Behaviour study spanning seven datasets and more than 880,000 texts found that LLM writing assistance can preserve what people mean while narrowing how differently they express it. Controlled rewrites reduced variation in writing complexity by roughly 21–50% and weakened some linguistic signals associated with author characteristics. That matters for systems that infer personality, identity or social context from text. The paper combines experimental rewriting with observational evidence, so not every population-level change can be attributed solely to LLM adoption.
attribution: Sourati et al. — Nature Human Behaviour

questionAndWhy: Can shared community memberships provide a measurable form of “common ground” between people who may never have interacted? This matters online because people routinely interpret short, context-heavy messages using assumptions about what members of a community already know.
whatTheyDid: Kumar and colleagues used Bluesky Starter Packs—user-curated lists organized around professions, places, identities, or interests—as community-affiliation labels. They analyzed 191,648 user pairs and compared shared community memberships with overlap in the users’ lexical repertoires, while separately accounting for proximity in the platform’s follow network.
whatTheyFound: Lexical similarity increased monotonically as users shared more Starter Packs; users sharing one pack were roughly twice as similar as equally connected strangers. The number of topically distinct shared communities was more informative than the raw number of overlapping packs, and community co-membership added information beyond follow-network proximity. The study is observational, and lexical overlap is a proxy for common ground rather than a direct measure of shared knowledge.
whatItMeans: Community affiliation can carry contextual information that ordinary pairwise network ties miss. For audience analysis, higher-order membership structures may help explain why the same phrase is interpreted differently across communities, but affiliation should not be treated as proof that two people hold the same beliefs or will respond similarly.
streamTitle: Shared online communities predicted a graded common language beyond simple follow-network proximity
streamSummary: A new Bluesky study used user-curated Starter Packs as community-affiliation labels and analyzed 191,648 user pairs. People who shared more communities also used more similar vocabularies, with one shared pack corresponding to roughly twice the lexical similarity of equally connected strangers. Topically distinct shared communities mattered more than raw overlap, and the pattern added information beyond ordinary follow-network distance. The study provides a scalable proxy for communal common ground, but it is observational and lexical overlap is not the same thing as directly demonstrating shared beliefs, knowledge, or persuasion susceptibility.

questionAndWhy: Has cockpit AI on a frontline fighter moved beyond laboratory work into flight testing, and what evidence is available about what the system actually does?
whatTheyDid: Dassault Aviation flight-tested two sovereign AI algorithms aboard a Rafale fighter. One was developed internally and one with Thales/cortAIx as part of an effort to integrate controlled and supervised AI into the cockpit in support of the human crew.
whatTheyFound: Dassault says both functions reached enough maturity to be eligible for future Rafale upgrades. The company did not disclose their operational roles, benchmark results, failure rates, safety test results, or human-workload effects. The announcement therefore demonstrates flight integration and maturation, not operational effectiveness.
whatItMeans: Moving AI onto an operational aircraft is a meaningful technology-readiness milestone, but it is not yet evidence of decision advantage. The next useful evidence would cover task definition, human authority, error handling, workload, contested-environment performance, and comparison with existing non-AI systems.
streamTitle: Dassault flight-tested two AI algorithms on Rafale—but has not disclosed what they do or how well they performed
streamSummary: Dassault Aviation says it has flight-tested two sovereign AI algorithms aboard the Rafale fighter, one developed internally and one with Thales/cortAIx. The company describes the effort as controlled and supervised cockpit AI serving the human crew and says the functions are mature enough to be considered for future upgrades. It has not disclosed the algorithms’ roles, performance, failure rates, safety results, or effects on pilot workload. The development is therefore a technology-integration milestone rather than evidence that AI has improved Rafale mission performance.

questionAndWhy: What are the consequences when a defense customer classifies an AI supplier as a national-security supply-chain risk?
whatTheyDid: Reuters reported a U.S. appeals-court ruling upholding the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk after a dispute over restrictions on autonomous weapons and mass surveillance uses.
whatTheyFound: The court ruling allowed the designation to stand at that stage, with major commercial and reputational consequences for the company; Anthropic disputed the decision.
whatItMeans: AI governance disputes can become procurement and supply-chain decisions, not merely model-policy debates. Legal rulings, government risk assessments, and technical safety evidence should remain distinct.
streamTitle: A U.S. appeals court upheld the Pentagon's supply-chain-risk designation of Anthropic
streamSummary: A U.S. appeals court upheld the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a national-security supply-chain risk, a decision with significant procurement and reputational consequences. The dispute centered partly on Anthropic's restrictions on certain military uses. The ruling resolves a legal stage, not the underlying technical question of whether the company's safeguards create operational risk or improve safety.

questionAndWhy: Can an equity-focused school intervention change observable student behavior, and do the expected process measures move with it?
whatTheyDid: The R-CITY trial randomized 27 schools to standard Second Step programming or Second Step plus equity-focused lessons, teacher coaching, and implementation support.
whatTheyFound: The added intervention improved one of six observed student-behavior outcomes—physical aggression—and one of three teacher-report outcomes—general teaching self-efficacy; most other measured outcomes were null.
whatItMeans: A meaningful behavioral effect can coexist with mostly null process measures. That makes it unsafe to assume a favored mediator or component caused the improvement.
streamTitle: One important behavior improved while most process measures stayed null
streamSummary: A 27-school cluster randomized trial found that adding R-CITY equity-focused lessons and teacher coaching to an existing social-emotional program improved one observed student outcome—physical aggression—and one teacher-reported outcome, while most other process and system measures did not significantly change. The result is valuable precisely because the nulls remain visible: a successful intervention package does not automatically reveal which component or mechanism produced the behavioral effect.

questionAndWhy: How can organizations quantify privacy risk inside a trained machine-learning model instead of treating privacy as a checklist? The study focuses on whether attack-based testing can create a practical risk score relevant to privacy-by-design decisions.
whatTheyDid: Han combined model-inversion, membership-inference, and attribute-inference attacks into a 0–100 privacy-risk methodology. The framework was tested across deep neural networks, decision trees, support-vector machines, and other model families using five standard benchmark datasets.
whatTheyFound: The method reported an average privacy-risk detection accuracy of 89.3% across its experiments. Deep neural networks produced higher mean risk scores in the tested setups (74.1) than ensemble approaches (51.6). These are benchmark results produced by a particular attack suite and scoring method; they do not constitute a legal determination of GDPR compliance or prove the same ranking will hold in a specific deployed system.
whatItMeans: Privacy can be evaluated empirically by trying to extract information from the model, not only by documenting governance controls. For PSYWERX-style AI TEVV, the useful pattern is to keep utility, privacy attack success, and organizational/legal compliance as separate dimensions rather than inferring one from another.
streamTitle: A new privacy-risk framework scores machine-learning models by how well common attacks can extract sensitive information
streamSummary: A Scientific Reports study proposes a 0–100 privacy-risk score built from three attack families: model inversion, membership inference, and attribute inference. Tested across multiple model architectures and five benchmark datasets, the method reported 89.3% average detection accuracy; deep neural networks had higher mean risk scores than ensemble approaches in the tested setups. The framework offers a practical way to make privacy testing more empirical, but its benchmark scores are not a legal judgment of GDPR compliance and may not transfer directly to a specific production environment. Utility, attack vulnerability, and governance still need separate assessment.

questionAndWhy: Does a changing maze slow problem solving or also stop people learning the optimal strategy?
whatTheyDid: A 132-person virtual-maze experiment compared fixed layouts with layouts changing across trials as participants searched for hidden coins.
whatTheyFound: Both groups improved; changing layouts slowed gains in route efficiency and completion time. A difference in optimal-strategy learning did not survive multiple-testing correction.
whatItMeans: Changing environments can slow task execution without clearly impairing underlying rule learning.
streamTitle: Changing mazes slowed navigation, not clearly rule learning
streamSummary: A virtual-maze study of 132 people showed reduced gains in route and time efficiency under changing layouts. The optimal-rule learning difference was inconclusive.

questionAndWhy: How is the Army testing counter-drone technologies against rising small-drone activity at the southern border?
whatTheyDid: Reuters reported a September Army exercise testing radars, autonomous guns, interceptor drones, and other counter-UAS systems in Arizona.
whatTheyFound: Officials cited 378 drone incursions in a month and 11 laser downings since August; the exercise itself did not provide controlled comparative effectiveness data for all systems.
whatItMeans: Operational testing should distinguish threat volume, system demonstrations, confirmed engagements, and comparative effectiveness.
streamTitle: The Army tested counter-drone systems at the southern border amid hundreds of reported incursions
streamSummary: Reuters reported U.S. Army counter-UAS testing in Arizona as cartel drone activity increased. Officials cited 378 incursions in the prior month and 11 drones downed by laser systems since August. The exercise tested a range of detection and defeat technologies, but public reporting did not establish comparative effectiveness across vendors or conditions. Field testing is an activity milestone, not a complete effectiveness assessment.

questionAndWhy: Can an agent explicitly guard its internal state against corruption during long workflows?
whatTheyDid: StateGuard introduced checks intended to detect or prevent unsafe state changes in agent trajectories.
whatTheyFound: The approach reduced some state-corruption failures on the reported benchmarks but remained dependent on the tested threat model.
whatItMeans: Persistent-agent security requires validating state transitions and provenance, not only screening initial prompts.
streamTitle: StateGuard targeted corruption of long-running agent state
streamSummary: StateGuard is a preprint approach for protecting persistent agent state during multi-step workflows. The reported tests reduced some state-corruption failures by checking transitions and maintaining stronger state controls. The results are benchmark-specific, but the architecture reinforces a broader security principle: long-running agents need protection for internal state as well as input filters.

questionAndWhy: Can simulated human participants be controlled through internal model representations rather than relying only on prompts that ask an LLM to “act like” someone? Prompt-based personas can be unstable and may not reveal what internal state is actually changing.
whatTheyDid: Zhang and colleagues extracted activation-space directions corresponding to 18 early maladaptive schemas from schema therapy. They tested whether an LLM’s projection onto those vectors tracked externally evaluated schema expression in its outputs, then directly shifted the internal activations along those directions to see whether the target schema became more strongly expressed.
whatTheyFound: Projection onto the extracted directions was associated with the corresponding schema expression, and linear intervention on the directions induced stronger expression in model outputs. The work shows controllable internal representation of these model behaviors; it does not establish that the vectors are equivalent to human psychological schemas or that the resulting agents reproduce human treatment responses.
whatItMeans: This is an important step from prompt engineering toward mechanistically controlled synthetic participants. For PSYWERX, the opportunity is to separate two validation questions: whether an internal manipulation reliably changes the model as intended, and whether that change is actually a valid proxy for variation in real humans.
streamTitle: Researchers directly manipulated internal LLM representations to create more controllable simulated participants
streamSummary: A new npj Artificial Intelligence study moves synthetic-human simulation beyond prompt-only personas. Researchers extracted internal activation-space directions corresponding to 18 early maladaptive schemas and found that projection onto those directions tracked schema-like expression in model outputs. Directly shifting activations along a target direction also increased the corresponding expression. That provides a more mechanistic and controllable way to alter model behavior. It does not show that the internal vectors are equivalent to human psychological traits or that manipulated LLMs will reproduce human experimental responses, so human-validity testing remains a separate requirement.
attribution: Zhang et al. — npj Artificial Intelligence

questionAndWhy: Political organizations often struggle to convert passive supporters into volunteers, and mass messages are cheap but easy to ignore. The researchers asked whether personal outreach that lets people express their own views changes real mobilization behavior.
whatTheyDid: Kamphorst and Larreguy partnered with a major left-wing party in the Netherlands for two preregistered field experiments before the 2021 general and 2022 municipal elections. More than 35,000 members in each study were randomized to receive a personal phone call, an email, or—where applicable—both, and the outcome was actual volunteer sign-up.
whatTheyFound: Phone calls increased volunteer sign-up from low baselines: roughly 0.89% to 1.6% in Study 1 and 0.22% to about 1.0% in Study 2, equivalent to relative increases of 83% and 361%. Emails alone had no detectable effect, and calls were especially effective among younger members. The authors interpret the opportunity to have one’s voice heard as important, but calls differ from emails in several ways, so “voice” is not isolated as the sole mechanism.
whatItMeans: Interactive contact can change real behavior where static outreach does not, but large relative gains should be read alongside the small absolute baseline rates. For influence and mobilization work, the study supports testing two-way interaction and perceived voice as design features rather than assuming more message exposure is sufficient.
streamTitle: Personal calls mobilized party volunteers where mass email did not
streamSummary: Two preregistered field experiments with a major Dutch political party randomized more than 35,000 members per study to personal calls, email or both and measured actual volunteer sign-up. Calls increased sign-up from low baselines—about 0.89% to 1.6% in one election and 0.22% to about 1.0% in the other—while email alone had no detectable effect. The relative increases were large, especially among younger members. The authors emphasize the chance to be heard, but calls differ from emails in more than “voice,” so that mechanism still needs cleaner isolation.

questionAndWhy: When people see a group opinion that differs from their own, is conformity just short-term compliance, or can it persist—and does persistence depend on whether the norm pushes behavior in a pro- or anti-climate direction?
whatTheyDid: Yeon and colleagues tested 47 Korean university students across 113 pro-climate behaviors. Participants first reported their own intentions, then saw experimentally generated peer norms that were congruent, moderately different, or highly different and either more pro-climate or less pro-climate. They rated their intentions again immediately and seven days later while EEG captured responses during the initial session.
whatTheyFound: Immediate conformity increased as the gap from the presented norm grew, regardless of whether the norm was pro- or anti-climate. Seven days later, conformity remained elevated for pro-climate norms but was not sustained for anti-climate norms. Stronger personal pro-climate norms predicted less conformity, and EEG responses also differed by norm direction. The sample was small, the peer opinions were synthetic, and the outcome was stated intention rather than observed behavior.
whatItMeans: Social influence can look symmetric in the moment and asymmetric over time. That makes persistence a separate outcome from immediate movement and suggests that the content of a norm can matter for whether compliance becomes internalized. The study is best treated as a mechanism probe, not evidence that one-week opinion shifts will translate into real-world climate behavior.
streamTitle: Social norms shifted climate intentions immediately in both directions, but only pro-climate shifts persisted
streamSummary: A small EEG experiment exposed 47 Korean university students to experimentally generated peer norms about 113 pro-climate behaviors. Participants moved their stated intentions toward both pro- and anti-climate group opinions immediately, especially when the group differed more from them. One week later, however, the shift remained for pro-climate norms but not anti-climate norms. Stronger personal norms reduced conformity. The study suggests short-term compliance and longer-term internalization may differ, but the sample was small, the peer opinions were synthetic, and the outcome was behavioral intention rather than observed behavior.

questionAndWhy: Are reward cues powerful because they automatically trigger learned behavior, or because people use them to infer which actions will pay off? Distinguishing the two changes how we explain habits and cue-driven decisions.
whatTheyDid: Huseynzade, Dignath and Eder conducted three human experiments using a stock-market task. Participants learned which cues and actions predicted monetary rewards. Later experiments introduced an instruction to disregard earlier cue learning after a simulated computer crash and imposed an additional working-memory task.
whatTheyFound: Cues biased choices toward associated rewards. The bias was stronger among participants reporting strategic use of cues; directed forgetting and memory load each reduced it. A small cue effect survived even when both manipulations discouraged deliberate cue use. The experiments cannot fully partition explicit inference from automatic association.
whatItMeans: Cue-driven action is not necessarily automatic. Beliefs about what a cue means, available attention and residual learned associations may jointly influence responses. This is a useful experimental warning against identifying one psychological mechanism from the same visible behavior.
streamTitle: Reward cues influenced choices less when people were told to forget them or had less working memory
streamSummary: Three experiments tested whether reward-associated cues guide behavior automatically or through conscious expectations. Participants first learned links among cues, actions, and monetary outcomes. A simulated software failure followed by instructions to disregard earlier cue learning substantially reduced cue-driven choices; a working-memory load also weakened the effect. Some response bias persisted despite both manipulations. This suggests that cue influence includes cognitive interpretation without ruling out automatic processes. The tasks involved artificial rewards, so their results should not be equated directly with persistent real-world habits or addictions.

questionAndWhy: What does a modern covert-action network look like when recruitment and surveillance are distributed across countries and intermediaries rather than carried out only by intelligence officers themselves?
whatTheyDid: The U.S. Justice Department unsealed an indictment charging five people it says were members of a Russian intelligence-services network. Prosecutors allege the network recruited people in the United States to surveil Russian dissidents, offered payments for killings, coordinated attack logistics in Europe, and proposed lower-level sabotage such as arson against warehouses or electrical infrastructure when recruits refused murder assignments.
whatTheyFound: The indictment describes a pipeline connecting recruitment, target surveillance, logistics, sabotage, and attempted murder-for-hire, including alleged offers of $40,000 to eliminate a U.S.-based dissident and $25,000 to kill a target in Lithuania. These are criminal allegations, not findings of guilt, and the defendants remain presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
whatItMeans: The case is useful for influence and hybrid-threat analysis because recruitment is not necessarily persuasion toward a worldview; it can be task-specific behavioral outsourcing through money, access, and social networks. Analysts should keep the alleged sponsor, recruiter, intermediary, task, target, and completed effect as separate layers of the operational chain.
streamTitle: A U.S. indictment maps an alleged Russian recruitment network from surveillance to sabotage and murder-for-hire
streamSummary: The U.S. Justice Department has charged five people it says belonged to a Russian intelligence-services network that recruited intermediaries for surveillance, sabotage, and targeted killings. Prosecutors allege U.S.-based recruits were offered money to surveil Russian dissidents and up to $40,000 for a killing, while other network activity included attack logistics in Europe and proposals to burn warehouses or attack electrical infrastructure. The case illustrates how covert influence can operate through paid behavioral recruitment rather than ideological persuasion. The indictment contains allegations, not convictions, and the defendants are presumed innocent.

questionAndWhy: Can FRAM represent the parallel, variable, sociotechnical work involved in surgical scheduling better than sequential process maps?
whatTheyDid: Rashid and colleagues used stakeholder interviews, observation, FRAM modeling, and FRAMalyse to represent 98 interconnected functions across the surgical scheduling pathway.
whatTheyFound: The model identified candidate high-variability and high-coupling functions, including surgical-team allocation and central patient management. These are modeled bottlenecks requiring further validation, not measured causal effects.
whatItMeans: FRAM is useful for making work-as-done, variability, and coordination explicit. Candidate leverage points should be validated with operational data before intervention.
streamTitle: A quantitative FRAM model mapped 98 functions in surgical scheduling and surfaced candidate bottlenecks
streamSummary: Researchers applied FRAM and FRAMalyse to a hospital surgical-scheduling process, using interviews and observations to model 98 interconnected functions. The analysis highlighted high-variability and high-coupling activities that could become bottlenecks. The model is a structured representation of sociotechnical work, not proof that changing the highest-ranked function will improve scheduling. Operational validation is the next step.
attribution: Rashid et al. — International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery

questionAndWhy: Which language features distinguish phishing texts from legitimate messages, and could those features make public scam warnings more concrete?
whatTheyDid: Researchers used systemic-functional linguistics to compare 106 Australian phishing text messages with 16 legitimate messages from organizations commonly impersonated in scams.
whatTheyFound: Phishing messages frequently combined urgent time limits, authority cues, instructions, and links. Time markers appeared in about 58% of scam messages and none of the small legitimate comparison set. The study analyzed text features, not recipients' susceptibility or prevention outcomes.
whatItMeans: Concrete linguistic examples may strengthen scam-awareness materials, but warning effectiveness and classifier performance still need testing with users and new messages.
streamTitle: Phishing texts used urgency and action cues absent from a small legitimate sample
streamSummary: A linguistic comparison of 106 scam texts and 16 legitimate texts found frequent urgency, authority, and link-related cues in scams. It did not test whether new warnings reduce victimization.
attribution: Kawabata — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

questionAndWhy: How should prediction systems be designed when people can change their behavior to manipulate the features an algorithm uses? This matters whenever a model influences consequential decisions and its rules become learnable or transparent.
whatTheyDid: Björkegren, Blumenstock, and Knight developed a prediction approach that explicitly models people’s incentives to manipulate observable features. They stress-tested the method in a large field experiment in Kenya and compared strategy-robust linear decision rules with conventional linear models such as LASSO.
whatTheyFound: The manipulation-aware rules outperformed standard linear prediction rules when people had incentives to respond strategically. The core contribution is not a new general-purpose causal model; it is a way to make prediction more stable when the prediction rule itself changes the behavior being measured.
whatItMeans: Once a score or model affects real decisions, the environment can adapt to the model. For PSYWERX, that is relevant to behavioral targeting, risk scoring, indicators, and monitoring systems: measures that become consequential can stop behaving like passive measurements.
streamTitle: Prediction models performed better when they anticipated how people would game them
streamSummary: An American Economic Review study develops ‘manipulation-robust’ prediction rules for settings where people can strategically change the features an algorithm observes. The authors explicitly model those incentives and stress-test the approach in a large field experiment in Kenya, where strategy-robust linear rules outperformed standard linear models such as LASSO.
